The Edo State Law Reform Commission has submitted a consolidated compilation of the state’s laws to the Chief Judge of Edo State, Justice Daniel Okungbowa, ending the state’s reliance on laws inherited from the defunct Bendel State. Receiving the document, titled Compendium of Laws of Edo State 2026, from the commission’s chairman on Thursday, the Chief Judge said previous administrations had made efforts to reform the old Bendel State laws but were unsuccessful. He expressed optimism that the consolidated laws had captured all relevant legislation in the state. Okungbowa, who commended the commission for what he described as a job well done, said the reform of the old Bendel State laws was long overdue, describing the presentation as a historic event. Earlier, the Chairman of the commission, Donald Osikhena-Boih, said the consolidated laws would make governance in the state seamless, adding that they would simplify the work of both the bench and the bar. He said, “On the part of the legislature, the lawmaking organ of government, when they have these laws on their shelves, before a bill is proposed, they will check whether the law exists, whether it has been in existence or whether it has been overtaken by events. “That alone gives them law audit, law accuracy and law pragmatism to know what and how to go about the lawmaking of the state.” Edo community leader calls for govt intervention in land dispute ADC, candidates rally supporters, allay disqualification fear Okpebholo promises end to excessive taxation in Edo On the executive arm, Osikhena-Boih said the consolidated laws would enable government officials to conduct proper legal audits before forwarding bills to the state House of Assembly. The chairman further said the availability of the consolidated laws would eliminate the excuse by members of the public that they were unaware of what the law provided. He explained that having the laws readily available would encourage citizens to familiarise themselves with relevant legislation and conduct themselves in accordance with the law. Speaking on the judiciary, the commission’s chairman noted that one of the biggest challenges facing the bench had been accessing and determining the applicability of existing laws. He added, “When the executive is making bills to be sent to the House of Assembly, they will go into the law audit, which is the Law Reform Commission, and particularly the law bank, to know which law is in existence with regard to what they try to cure that is considered to be a vacuum in the state. “Then going to the judiciary, and of course you know very, very well that the most herculean task the judiciary, the bench, has always faced is getting the laws articulated, or rather making the law applicable. “If you know that the laws are in place, you want to be careful and be orderly in society. You visit the law so that in the areas of your endeavour, you will not commit unnecessary infractions of the law.” Adeyinka Adedipe
